The inspiration of these two methods comes from recent ﬁndings that curriculum can help when noisy data are present (50; 31; 41). We believe data points of future task can be viewed as noisy interference for samples stored in M. In these two policies, curricular easy points of each task are picked as candidates for M. E.1 Algorithm Curricular Easy Samples We rank data examples from easy to hard based on the implicit cur- ricula (50). Speciﬁcally, we ﬁrst record the learned epochs as an attribute of an example, which is the earliest epoch in training where a model correctly predicts this example for that and subsequent epochs till now. As the learned epoch is a positive integer attribute, it is deﬁned as a subset of the totally ordered set Z+. We also record the current loss of each example as another attribute. The loss attribute is deﬁned as a subset of the totally ordered set R. The ranking of examples is based on the lexicographical order on the Cartesian product of the two attributes, i.e., ﬁrst sorting the examples by the learned epoch attribute, and then ordering examples within the same ranked epoch by their losses. As a result, each training example of a task would be associated with an unique ranking. Also, the ranking would be updated after each epoch. ER-CurRes The ER-CurRes algorithm is shown in Algorithm. 4. Different from ER-Res which stores examples sampled from the whole distribution Pi of a task ti (11), we sample subset of data points from an “easy pool”, i.e. Peasy i . The size is calculated by the dataset size |Di|multiplying a hyperparameter γ, whose value is reported for each evaluation dataset in Section F. Compared to taking the top few easiest points of each class, sampling from the pool utilizes the beneﬁts of randomness (4; 50). Suppose we train a total of k epochs of task ti, in order to obtain a smooth transition and the samples based on a more stable curriculum ranking, we take the examples obeying ER-Res policy (i.e., samples from Pi) for the ﬁrst ⌈k/2⌉epochs, and take the examples obeying ER-CurRes policy (i.e., samples from Peasy i ) for the last ⌊k/2⌋epochs. When we ﬁnish training, we replace the examples of task ti in the memory which are not from Peasy i . ER-CurRing-Full Likewise, as shown in Algorithm. 5, ER-CurRing-Full follows the ER-Ring- Full strategy in the ﬁrst ⌈k/2⌉epochs to ﬁll a FIFO memory ( 11). After that, we substitute the memory slots with points from the easy pool of each observed class. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, particularly for experience replay (ER) methods that typically use static memory construction. It formulates dynamic memory construction in ER as a combinatorial optimization problem to directly minimize the global loss across all experienced tasks. The main contribution is the Global Pseudo-task Simulation (GPS) method, an approximate solution for online continual learning that mimics future catastrophic forgetting by permuting data to create pseudo-tasks. GPS consistently improves accuracy across four vision benchmarks, is close to an offline optimal solution, and serves as a unified framework to enhance existing ER-based memory construction policies.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The core methodology involves formulating dynamic memory construction as a combinatorial optimization problem to minimize global loss. An offline solution is first derived using three tactics to reduce the search space: (1) an equal memory heuristic, (2) a base policy assumption (mixing ER-Res for random samples and ER-Ring-Full for class-balanced samples via a 'switching point'), and (3) the existence of a unique switching point to enable binary search. For the online setting, Global Pseudo-task Simulation (GPS) is proposed. GPS synthesizes pseudo-future tasks by permuting pixels of current task images to mimic forgetting patterns, chosen because permutation generates tasks with similar difficulty and limited zero-shot transfer ability, aligning with real-world benchmarks. It then uses a binary search algorithm on these pseudo-tasks and pseudo-memories to find approximate switching points that optimize the global objective (specifically the loss of the current task over simulated future steps). For efficiency, simulations use fewer examples and training epochs, and a sliding window approach is used for long task sequences.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: The research evaluates GPS on four widely used vision benchmarks: P-MNIST (10 tasks), S-CIFAR-10 (5 tasks with 2 classes each), S-CIFAR-100 (10 tasks with 10 classes each), and TinyImageNet (10 tasks with 20 classes each). For P-MNIST, a fully connected network with two 100-unit ReLU hidden layers is used. For S-CIFAR-10, S-CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet, Resnet18 is employed. Baselines include ER-Res, ER-Ring-Full, ER-Hybrid, and non-ER methods such as online EWC (oEWC), iCaRL, A-GEM, GSS, and OGD, as well as an 'ER-Oracle' representing the offline optimal solution. Training uses SGD with a 0.1 learning rate and a memory loss factor (λ) of 1. Epochs range from 5 (P-MNIST) to 100 (S-CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet), with batch sizes of 10 or 50. All results are averaged over 5 runs with error bars. Additional experiments include evaluations on long task sequences (20 and 40 tasks for P-MNIST), analysis of different pseudo-task synthesis methods (permutation, rotation, blurring), and integration with advanced ER variants like DER++ and HAL.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The current work focuses exclusively on task- and domain-incremental learning setups. The proposed GPS method does not show significant improvement when the memory buffer size is very small, mainly because the optimal memory construction tends towards a pure ER-Ring-Full policy (switching point near 1), and the base policy assumption may not hold as well under such limited memory conditions. The paper explicitly states that no potential negative societal impacts were observed from their perspective.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future work will explore extending Global Pseudo-task Simulation (GPS) to the class-incremental (class-IL) setup. This transition presents two challenges: handling the unknown task identity (potentially by triggering simulation after a certain amount of data points rather than tasks) and possibly requiring more complex mixture policies (beyond ER-Res and ER-Ring-Full) and new assumptions to find the offline oracle for class-IL. Additionally, the authors hope to inspire the community to design new datasets that better reﬂect real-world scenarios, such as those with specific zero-shot transfer patterns, where inferred biases could be injected into the simulation process.
